meta.location: Dwarakanath Bhavan, Shree Ram Mandir complex, Katrak Road, Wadala, Mumbai 400031
meta.foundedNote: The Samiti and host temple both date this annual Ganeshotsav to 1955; this does not date the permanent Ram temple.
meta.intro: Wadala's GSB Ganeshotsav is organised by G.S.B. Sarvajanik Ganeshotsava Samiti at Dwarakanath Bhavan in the Shree Ram Mandir complex. Its annual Mahaganapati, known devotionally as Navasacha Suvarna Ganapati, belongs to a festival traced to 1955. The extended cycle of Vedic sevas, communal meals and Anant Chaturdashi observance makes it distinct from King's Circle's GSB Seva Mandal. This foundation records rituals and community work without treating the host Ram temple's institutional history as a history of a permanent Ganesh idol.

paragraphs.text: Both the Samiti and the host temple trace the public festival at Dwarakanath Bhavan to 1955. Its address is Katrak Road, Wadala. Although the host temple website also uses a broader Dadar description in its footer, the named festival venue and contact address are Wadala. This is a separate organising body from GSB Seva Mandal at King's Circle.

The temporary Ganapati is installed within an established Ram temple complex associated with followers of Gokarn Partagali Jeevottam Muth. Annual Ganesh worship should be catalogued separately from the temple's permanent deities, buildings and Ram Navami history. The host institution describes the festival as a setting for worship and social participation across community boundaries.

The Samiti's ritual list includes Ganahoma, Mooda Ganapati, Tulabhar, Anna Santarpana, Ranga Pooja and Atharvashirsha recitation. Several sevas explicitly exclude Ekadashi. Its 2026 appeal announces twelve days from Ganesh Chaturthi to Anant Chaturdashi, 14-25 September. The duration should follow each annual calendar rather than be reduced to a fixed eleven-day formula.

The host temple describes an Ananta observance involving a kalash, darbha form, Saligram and a fourteen-knotted thread, subsequently immersed with the festival Ganapati. Community care is also visible in recent records: GSBS Medical Trust reports a 3 September 2025 camp with more than 151 attendees, alongside a separate child-health event that festival. These records document festival activity without substituting service photographs for a portrait of its deity. A 2017 community periodical also records health and recitation programmes, establishing that this service component predates the recent photographs.

sections.title: A separate Wadala sequence, including the interrupted festival

paragraphs.text: The 2008 community report explicitly places the54th festival at Dwarakanath Bhavan in the Ram Mandir complex and traces the first public celebration to 1955. It describes clay-idol practice alongside food distribution, educational aid and medical work. Its lost image links are a real archival gap: the surviving text cannot be converted into a photographed 2008 idol.

Arun Shanbhag's 2009 photo essay is especially useful because it separates household worship, King's Circle and Wadala. His 2011 Wadala post adds a scene of priests working beside the ornamented idol, supported by original attachment metadata. The 2009 Photobucket overlay is retained, and the 2012 Rediff section is assigned here because it specifically says Ram Mandir Wadala despite its generic GSB header.

The 2015 visitor photograph has embedded 2015 camera metadata consistent with its contemporary post, while the 2016 and 2018 roundups separately name and credit their Wadala frames. Bellevision's 2017 event report links the63rd festival to the presence of the Gokarna Partagali mutt's spiritual heads. These annual-festival records are kept distinct from the history of the permanent host temple.

The pandemic interruption was institution-specific. A25 May 2020 announcement postponed Wadala's Bhadrapad festival to the following Maghi season. In February 2021, organisers described a much smaller proposed one-day observance: an18-inch idol, online pujas and immersion on the premises, without public darshan or prasad distribution. These are dated reported plans; neither source proves every planned action was completed.

The openly licensed 2022 original offers unusually detailed provenance: the uploader identifies both Wadala and the depicted year, and the physical throne carries the institution's name. Its text and camera metadata disagree by one day but agree on 2022. The archive therefore preserves the year with the discrepancy disclosed, rather than choosing an exact date or using the 2023 upload as the event year.

researchNotes.coverage: Samiti notices and rituals, host temple account, 2017 community periodical, medical-trust reports and a directly attributed 2024 visitor photograph. Three dated media inspected: an idol photograph, service scene and announcement graphic. Phase 2: 11 annual entries supplemented after direct image inspection; source labels and photographic appearance assessed separately.
gaps: No idol photographs before 2009 obtained;2008 contemporary report survives but tested image links return404.
The 2012 contributor-blog sequence had ambiguous photo associations, including a visible Mumbaicha Raja banner; none of those frames was assigned to Wadala.
May 2020 postponement and February 2021 plans do not establish completion; actual pandemic observance photos and post-event records are still needed.
2011 procession photographs credited Amol Kamat are a promising public-post lead, but the tested original returned403and no unviewed image was added.
Most years still lack named sculptor contracts or original institution-held annual albums.
The 2022 uploader date and camera/GPS day differ by one day;2022 is supported, an exact day is not resolved.
New photographs retain unknown reuse permission except the specifically documented Heshanbhag Commons CC BY-SA 4.0original.
